inputs.need:
I am a physiotherapist and I coordinate a community falls prevention exercise programme that our health region runs in 14 community centres. Adults aged 65 and over who have fallen, or who are referred by their family doctor, join a 24-week group programme of strength and balance exercise twice a week, with home exercises in between. The programme only works if people keep coming, but attendance drops sharply after about week six: last year only 38 percent of the 520 people who started attended at least two thirds of the sessions, and few do the home exercises. People tell us the reasons are transport, pain, exercises that feel too easy or too hard, and losing the habit after a missed week.

We want to run a pragmatic trial of an adherence support package added to the usual programme: a weekly text or phone reminder, two calls from a trained peer volunteer who has completed the programme, and a home exercise booklet with a tick calendar that the instructor reviews every four weeks. Participants would be allocated individually by chance to the usual programme or the programme with support, in all 14 centres, and the instructors would deliver the classes as they do now. The main question is whether attendance and home exercise improve; falls matter most, but I doubt we can show a difference in falls with our numbers.

I need help choosing the primary outcome, the sample size, how to allocate people without disrupting the groups, and what the evidence says about adherence support in exercise programmes, because my first searches found almost nothing.
inputs.constraints: No research funding beyond the programme budget. Instructors cannot take on extra data collection; attendance comes from the existing class registers. Peer volunteers are unpaid and trained by the programme. The support package must also work for people without a mobile phone.
localFacts: Last year 520 people started the 24-week programme in 14 community centres; 38 percent attended at least two thirds of the 48 sessions.
The regional falls programme manager approved adding the adherence package and central allocation for the 2027 intakes (approval FPM-2027-03, dated 2026-09-12).
Twelve former participants have volunteered to be trained as peer supporters.
No research ethics board application has been made yet.

records.title: Telephone and text support for attendance at community strength and balance classes: a pragmatic trial
records.authors: Lindberg-Okafor A, Marsh-Venkataraman T, Oduya-Clarke P
records.venue: Kestrelmoor Journal of Ageing and Activity
records.abstract: We allocated 412 adults aged 65 and over who were joining community strength and balance classes either to usual classes or to classes with weekly text or phone reminders and a call after any missed week. Attendance at two thirds or more of sessions over 24 weeks was 54 percent with support and 41 percent with usual classes. Falls over 12 months did not differ between groups (rate ratio 0.94, 95 percent CI 0.71 to 1.25). Participants valued calls more than texts, and people without a mobile phone received calls only. The trial was not blinded, and instructors knew which participants received support.

records.title: Peer volunteer calls and home exercise after falls prevention classes: a controlled comparison in community programmes
records.abstract: Two community falls prevention programmes offered participants two calls from a trained peer volunteer, a former participant, while a third programme did not. Home exercise diaries were completed on at least three days a week by 62 percent of participants who received peer calls and 35 percent of those who did not. Attendance at classes was similar in the three programmes. Peer volunteers reported that the calls were rewarding but that some participants were hard to reach. Programmes were not allocated at random, the diaries were self-reported, and the programme that offered no calls served an older population.

response.synthesis: Two retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; the five earlier items remain unverified leads and are not part of the certainty. One trial found that reminders and calls after missed weeks raised attendance from 41 to 54 percent without a detectable effect on falls, and a non-random comparison linked peer volunteer calls with more home exercise. The evidence is thin but directly relevant, and it supports attendance as the primary outcome with home exercise as secondary and falls reported descriptively.
response.gradeRationale: Two studies only, one unblinded trial and one non-random comparison; consistent direction but imprecise and indirect for peer calls.

response.reading: Attendance falls after week six for reasons outside the classes: transport, pain, difficulty level and broken habits. Reminders and calls after missed weeks target the broken habit (c1); peer calls target home exercise (c2); neither has been shown to prevent falls at this scale (c3). Class registers already record attendance, which keeps the trial inside usual practice.

response.overview: Pragmatic trial with individual allocation by a central office, in the 2027 intakes of a 24-week community strength and balance programme in 14 centres, comparing usual classes with classes plus an adherence support package.
response.population: Adults aged 65 and over starting the programme in 2027 who consent; people without a mobile phone and people with limited English are included, with phone calls and interpreters.
response.exposure: Adherence support package: weekly reminder by text or phone, a call within three days of any missed week, two calls from a trained peer volunteer (weeks 3 and 8), and a home exercise tick calendar reviewed by the instructor every four weeks.
response.procedures: After consent at the first class, the central office allocates each participant by computer-generated sequence stratified by centre, and informs the reminder coordinator; instructors see the calendar only for supported participants. Attendance comes from class registers; home exercise from the calendar (supported) and a two-question phone check at weeks 12 and 24 (both groups); falls from a monthly falls calendar returned by post or phone.

response.designSummary: Two-arm pragmatic trial with individual allocation stratified by centre; binary primary outcome at 24 weeks.
response.sampleSize: With 38 percent attending two thirds of sessions under usual classes and a smallest worthwhile difference of 12 percentage points (to 50 percent), 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 needs about 268 participants per arm, 536 in total. Allowing 10 percent who consent but never attend a class after allocation gives about 596. At about 43 new participants a month, recruitment takes about 14 months of 2027 and early 2028 intakes. Falls: with about 0.9 falls per person-year, the trial cannot detect a plausible reduction and falls are reported with a rate ratio and its interval, not tested.
response.primaryAnalysis: Logistic regression of attendance at two thirds of sessions on arm, adjusted for centre and age group, intention to treat; the risk difference with its 95 percent confidence interval is reported alongside the odds ratio.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Home exercise days by linear regression at weeks 12 and 24; falls as a rate ratio from negative binomial regression with its interval; delivery proportions; injuries and pain flares described by arm.
response.missingData: Attendance is complete from registers; missing phone checks and falls calendars are handled by multiple imputation under missing at random, with a sensitivity analysis assuming worse outcomes for non-responders.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary outcomes reported with intervals and labelled as secondary.
response.software: R; the statistical analysis plan archived before the first allocation.
overfittingGuards: Two adjustment variables fixed in advance
No subgroup analyses beyond sex and phone ownership, both pre-specified
response.summary: About 268 participants per arm for a 12-point difference in attendance; falls descriptive.

response.risks: Low: participants receive the usual programme, with or without reminders and calls. Risks are unwanted contact, pressure to attend when unwell, and peer volunteers hearing personal information.
response.consent: Written informed consent at the first class before allocation; participants may stop reminders or calls at any time without leaving the programme.
response.data: Registers and calendars are held by the programme with study numbers; peer volunteers sign a confidentiality agreement and see only a name and phone number.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: people without a mobile phone, people with limited English, people living alone and people without transport are least likely to attend. Phone calls replace texts where needed, interpreters are used for calls, and attendance is reported by phone ownership and language.
response.effectiveness: The trial answers whether the package is worth adding to the programme's standard offer.
response.efficiency: Reminders and calls use existing staff and volunteers; attendance data already exist.
response.costs: Coordinator time for reminders, volunteer training and phone costs, within the programme budget.
response.grants: None needed for the trial; a positive result could support regional funding for the package.
response.partnerships: Twelve peer volunteers, instructors from the 14 centres, and an older adults' advisory group.
response.rebPath: Research ethics board application to be submitted, following ICH-GCP and the Declaration of Helsinki; no allocation begins before approval.
response.limitations: Unblinded; contamination within classes; falls underpowered.
response.summary: Low-risk pragmatic trial with written consent, equal access to classes, and equity reporting by phone ownership and language.

response.partnershipPlan: The older adults' advisory group reviews the reminder wording and the peer call script; two peer volunteers help design the volunteer training.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; programme feedback forms from last year are read for reasons people stopped attending.

response.title: Adherence support for a community falls prevention exercise programme: a pragmatic trial in 14 centres
response.abstract: Objective: to test whether reminders, missed-week calls, peer volunteer calls and a home exercise calendar increase attendance at a 24-week community strength and balance programme. Design: pragmatic trial with individual allocation stratified by centre. Primary outcome: attendance at 32 or more of 48 sessions. Results will follow the trial.
response.introduction: Community strength and balance programmes prevent falls only if people keep attending. A recorded search found one trial of reminders and one comparison of peer calls; other suggested studies were unverified leads.
response.methods: Central allocation after consent, usual classes and instructors, register-based attendance, phone checks for home exercise, monthly falls calendars, intention-to-treat analysis.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present recruitment, delivery of the package, attendance by arm with the risk difference, secondary outcomes and falls.
response.discussion: The discussion will consider contamination within classes, who the package reached, and why falls were not powered.
response.limitations: Unblinded; contamination; self-reported home exercise and falls.
response.conclusion: To be written after the trial.
response.reportingChecklist: CONSORT extension for pragmatic trials with TIDieR
response.summary: CONSORT-structured draft with results left empty.
